name: Crater Lake National Park
note: A collapsed volcano holding the deepest lake in the United States. Roosevelt signed the bill creating the park on May 22, 1902.

name: Wind Cave National Park
note: The first national park anywhere created to protect a cave. Roosevelt signed the act on January 9, 1903.

name: Sully's Hill National Park
note: A wooded hill above Devils Lake, reserved by Roosevelt's proclamation of June 2, 1904. It became a game preserve in 1931 and, at the Spirit Lake Tribe's request, was renamed White Horse Hill National Game Preserve in 2019.
today: White Horse Hill National Game Preserve

name: Mesa Verde National Park
note: The first national park set aside to preserve the works of people: the cliff dwellings and mesa-top villages of the Ancestral Puebloans. Roosevelt signed the act on June 29, 1906.

name: Platt National Park
note: Mineral and freshwater springs at Sulphur. Roosevelt signed the 1902 act creating the Sulphur Springs Reservation and the 1906 resolution renaming it Platt National Park. Since 1976 it has been part of Chickasaw National Recreation Area.

name: Devils Tower National Monument
note: The first national monument, proclaimed under the brand-new Antiquities Act. The proclamation called the tower 'such an extraordinary example of the effect of erosion in the higher mountains as to be a natural wonder.'

name: El Morro National Monument
note: A sandstone bluff where centuries of travelers, from Ancestral Puebloans to Spanish and American passersby, carved their marks.

name: Montezuma Castle National Monument
note: A five-story Sinagua cliff dwelling tucked into a limestone cliff above Beaver Creek.

name: Petrified Forest National Monument
note: Fallen logs from ancient forests, turned to stone and scattered across the painted desert. It became a national park in 1962.

name: Chaco Canyon National Monument
note: Great houses like Pueblo Bonito made this canyon the center of the Ancestral Puebloan world. Today it is Chaco Culture National Historical Park.

name: Lassen Peak National Monument
note: The volcano at the southern end of the Cascade Range. Its eruptions of 1914 to 1917 helped make it the heart of Lassen Volcanic National Park in 1916.

name: Cinder Cone National Monument
note: A cone of volcanic cinders beside a lava field, Snag Lake and Lake Bidwell, set aside for what it shows about the region's volcanoes. Now part of Lassen Volcanic National Park.

name: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument
note: Mogollon homes built into cliff caves above a fork of the Gila River. The proclamation called them 'the best representative of the Cliff-Dwellers' remains of that region.'

name: Tonto National Monument
note: Salado cliff dwellings that today look out over Theodore Roosevelt Lake, the reservoir behind Roosevelt Dam.

name: Muir Woods National Monument
note: Old-growth coast redwoods given to the nation by William and Elizabeth Thacher Kent, the first monument created on donated land. It was named for John Muir.

name: Grand Canyon National Monument
note: Roosevelt stood at the rim in 1903 and said: "Leave it as it is. You cannot improve on it. The ages have been at work on it, and man can only mar it." (Remarks at the Grand Canyon, May 6, 1903.) It became a national park in 1919.

name: Pinnacles National Monument
note: Volcanic spires and talus caves in the Gabilan Mountains. It became Pinnacles National Park in 2013.

name: Jewel Cave National Monument
note: A cave lined with sparkling calcite crystals in the Black Hills, now known to be one of the longest caves in the world.

name: Natural Bridges National Monument
note: Three great stone bridges carved by White Canyon and its streams. Utah's first national monument.

name: Lewis and Clark Cavern National Monument
note: A limestone cavern above the Jefferson River. Congress transferred it to Montana in 1937; it is now Lewis and Clark Caverns State Park.
today: Lewis and Clark Caverns State Park (Montana)

name: Tumacácori National Monument
note: Ruins of a Spanish colonial mission church on the Santa Cruz River, now Tumacácori National Historical Park.

name: Wheeler National Monument
note: Eroded spires of volcanic tuff high in the San Juan Mountains. Congress abolished the monument in 1950; it is now the Wheeler Geologic Area of Rio Grande National Forest.
today: Wheeler Geologic Area, Rio Grande National Forest

name: Mount Olympus National Monument
note: Proclaimed two days before Roosevelt left office, to protect glaciers and the summer range of the Olympic elk, named Cervus roosevelti in his honor. It became Olympic National Park in 1938.

name: Yellowstone National Park
note: The first national park, signed into law by President Ulysses S. Grant on March 1, 1872.

name: Sequoia National Park
note: Created to protect giant sequoias. A second act a week later, on October 1, 1890, roughly tripled its size.

name: General Grant National Park
note: Four sections around the General Grant Tree. It was folded into Kings Canyon National Park in 1940.

name: Yosemite National Park
note: In 1890 the park surrounded, but did not include, Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove, which California held. Roosevelt signed the joint resolution of June 11, 1906, that brought them into the national park.

name: Mount Rainier National Park
note: A glacier-wrapped volcano set aside about two and a half years before Roosevelt became president.

name: Pelican Island Reservation
note: A 5.5-acre island in the Indian River Lagoon became the first federal bird reservation, the seed of today's National Wildlife Refuge System. Roosevelt enlarged it on January 26, 1909.

name: Breton Island Reservation
note: Barrier islands off the Mississippi delta where terns and pelicans nest; Roosevelt came to see it for himself in 1915.

name: Stump Lake Reservation
note: North Dakota's first federal bird reservation: about 27 acres of islands in a prairie lake, still a refuge today.

name: Huron Islands Reservation
note: Rocky granite islands in Lake Superior where gulls nest, now also protected as wilderness.

name: Siskiwit Islands Reservation
note: Small gull-nesting islands in Siskiwit Bay off Isle Royale, which lie inside Isle Royale National Park today.

name: Passage Key Reservation
note: A shifting sand key at the mouth of Tampa Bay where seabirds and shorebirds nest.

name: Indian Key Reservation
note: A small mangrove key in lower Tampa Bay set aside for nesting water birds.

name: Tern Islands Reservation
note: Low sandy islands near the mouth of the Mississippi River set aside for nesting terns.

name: Shell Keys Reservation
note: Tiny shell islands in the Gulf south of Marsh Island, among the smallest refuges in the system.

name: Three Arch Rocks Reservation
note: Sea stacks off Oceanside, Oregon, crowded with common murres, tufted puffins and sea lions.
today: Three Arch Rocks National Wildlife Refuge

name: Flattery Rocks Reservation
note: Rocks and islets off the northwest tip of Washington, one of three Olympic coast seabird refuges Roosevelt created on the same day.

name: Quillayute Needles Reservation
note: Rugged sea stacks off La Push where seabirds nest by the thousands.

name: Copalis Rock Reservation
note: Offshore rocks and reefs on the central Washington coast set aside for nesting seabirds.

name: East Timbalier Island Reservation
note: A Gulf barrier island set aside for nesting terns and pelicans; the reservation was revoked in 1969 as the island eroded.

name: Mosquito Inlet Reservation
note: Islets in today's Ponce de Leon Inlet, enlarged in 1909 and revoked in 1928.

name: Tortugas Keys Reservation
note: The Dry Tortugas, famous for huge colonies of sooty and noddy terns, became part of Fort Jefferson National Monument in 1935 and are now a national park.

name: Key West Reservation
note: Mangrove islands west of Key West, a winter haven for wading birds and seabirds.

name: Klamath Lake Reservation
note: Marshes around Lower Klamath Lake, often called the nation's first refuge set aside for waterfowl.

name: Lake Malheur Reservation
note: A vast high-desert marsh where plume hunters had been killing egrets and grebes before the reservation.

name: Chase Lake Reservation
note: Home to one of North America's largest nesting colonies of American white pelicans.

name: Pine Island Reservation
note: Mangrove islands in Pine Island Sound where herons, egrets and pelicans nest.

name: Palma Sola Reservation
note: A small bird island in Palma Sola Bay near Bradenton; the reservation was revoked in 1948, apparently after the island washed away.

name: Matlacha Pass Reservation
note: Mangrove islands between Pine Island and the mainland, created the same day as Palma Sola.

name: Island Bay Reservation
note: Mangrove islands near Cape Haze that shelter nesting wading birds.

name: Loch Katrine Reservation
note: A reservoir site in the Oregon Basin near Cody, about 5,500 acres; revoked in 1921.

name: Hawaiian Islands Reservation
note: A string of remote islands and reefs northwest of Kauai, including Laysan and French Frigate Shoals, where millions of seabirds nest.
today: Hawaiian Islands National Wildlife Refuge (within Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument)

name: Salt River Reservation
note: Land around the new Roosevelt Dam reservoir, one of 17 reclamation reservoirs made bird reservations in a single order on February 25, 1909; revoked in 1961.

name: East Park Reservation
note: A reclamation reservoir in the Coast Range foothills; revoked in 1921.

name: Deer Flat Reservation
note: Lake Lowell near Nampa, still a refuge and a major stop for migrating ducks and geese.

name: Minidoka Reservation
note: Lake Walcott on the Snake River; re-designated as a wildlife refuge in 1936 and still protected today.

name: Willow Creek Reservation
note: A reclamation reservoir near Augusta, Montana; revoked in 1968 and handed to the Bureau of Reclamation.

name: Carlsbad Reservation
note: Reservoirs on the Pecos River above Carlsbad; revoked in 1947.

name: Rio Grande Reservation
note: Elephant Butte Reservoir; converted to a wildlife refuge in 1933 and revoked in 1947.

name: Cold Springs Reservation
note: A reservoir near Hermiston that still draws ducks, geese and bald eagles.

name: Belle Fourche Reservation
note: Orman Dam's reservoir near Belle Fourche; revoked in 1964.

name: Strawberry Valley Reservation
note: Strawberry Reservoir in the Wasatch high country; revoked in 1961.

name: Keechelus Reservation
note: A Cascade mountain lake dammed for irrigation; revoked in 1921.

name: Kachess Reservation
note: A Cascade mountain lake dammed for irrigation; revoked in 1921.

name: Clealum Reservation
note: Cle Elum Lake in the Cascades; revoked in 1921.

name: Bumping Lake Reservation
note: A Cascade reservoir east of Mount Rainier; revoked in 1921.

name: Conconully Reservation
note: A reservoir in the Okanogan highlands; revoked in 1960.

name: Pathfinder Reservation
note: Pathfinder Reservoir on the North Platte; revoked in 1922 but restored as a bird refuge in 1928.

name: Shoshone Reservation
note: The Shoshone (now Buffalo Bill) Reservoir west of Cody; revoked in 1922.

name: Bering Sea Reservation
note: St. Matthew, Hall and Pinnacle islands, far out in the Bering Sea and thick with seabirds.

name: Tuxedni Reservation
note: Chisik and Duck islands in Cook Inlet, nesting grounds for puffins, kittiwakes and murres.

name: Saint Lazaria Reservation
note: A small volcanic island off Sitka where storm-petrels nest in burrows by the hundreds of thousands.

name: Yukon Delta Reservation
note: Millions of acres of tundra between the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers; revoked in 1922, and the same country is now part of the Yukon Delta National Wildlife Refuge.

name: Culebra Reservation
note: Islands off Puerto Rico's east coast where sooty terns, boobies and tropicbirds nest.

name: Farallon Reservation
note: Rocky islands west of the Golden Gate, the largest seabird colony in the lower 48 states.

name: Pribilof Reservation
note: Walrus and Otter islands in the Pribilofs; handed to the Bureau of Fisheries in 1910 and later folded into Alaska Maritime refuge.

name: Bogoslof Reservation
note: A restless volcanic island in the Aleutians, Roosevelt's last bird reservation, made just before he left office.

name: Wichita Game Preserve
note: Roosevelt turned the Wichita Forest Reserve into a game preserve, and Bronx Zoo bison arrived in 1907 to restart a wild herd.

name: Grand Canyon Game Preserve
note: The Kaibab Plateau north of the Grand Canyon, set aside to protect its deer.
today: Kaibab National Forest (North Kaibab Ranger District) and part of Grand Canyon National Park

name: National Bison Range
note: Congress created this range to save one of the last bison herds, and the land has since been returned to the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes.
today: Bison Range (held in trust for the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes)

name: Fire Island Reservation
note: An island in Cook Inlet near today's Anchorage where cow moose came to have their calves.

name: Salt River Project
note: One of the first five projects; Roosevelt came back in March 1911 to dedicate the stone dam that carries his name.

name: Truckee-Carson Project
note: Derby Dam turned Truckee River water into a canal bound for the Carson desert, and the main Truckee canal was finished in June 1905.

name: Uncompahgre Valley Project
note: Crews bored a tunnel about six miles through solid rock to carry Gunnison River water into the Uncompahgre Valley.

name: Milk River Project
note: This project planned to borrow water from the St. Mary River near Glacier and send it down the Milk River to farms on Montana's Hi-Line.

name: North Platte Project
note: Pathfinder Dam stores North Platte water in Wyoming, and the Interstate Canal carries it to farms in western Nebraska.

name: Shoshone Project
note: A 328-foot concrete arch dam in the canyon above Cody holds the Shoshone River for farms around Powell.

name: Minidoka Project
note: Minidoka Dam on the Snake River was finished in 1906 and created Lake Walcott.

name: Yuma Project
note: Laguna Dam spans the Colorado River above Yuma and was finished in March 1909.

name: Lower Yellowstone Project
note: A low rock-and-timber weir near Intake, Montana, sends Yellowstone River water to farms reaching into North Dakota.

name: Belle Fourche Project
note: An earthen dam 115 feet high and more than a mile long on Owl Creek stores Belle Fourche River water for western South Dakota farms.

name: Hondo Project
note: Engineers built a reservoir near Roswell, but the water seeped into the ground, and the project never delivered much.

name: Boise Project
note: The Boise River Diversion Dam, finished in 1908, sends river water into the New York Canal for the Boise Valley.

name: Huntley Project
note: Opened on land ceded by the Crow Tribe, this Yellowstone River project east of Billings first delivered water in 1908.

name: Klamath Project
note: Klamath engineers drained lakebeds and marshes along the Oregon-California line for farmland, and Clear Lake Dam was finished in January 1910.

name: Garden City Project
note: Kansas's only early project pumped groundwater from under the Arkansas River, but farmers stopped paying their charges and the pumps went quiet by 1910.

name: Okanogan Project
note: An earthen dam on Salmon Creek above Okanogan stored water for orchards in north-central Washington.

name: Umatilla Project
note: Cold Springs Dam, finished in June 1908, stores Umatilla River water for farms around Hermiston in northeastern Oregon.

name: Yakima Project
note: The government bought and rebuilt the old Sunnyside canal, and its first water reached farms in 1907.

name: Strawberry Valley Project
note: A tunnel about 3½ miles long sends water from the Colorado River basin west to farms around Spanish Fork.

name: Williston Project
note: Steam power pumped Missouri River water uphill to farms around Williston.
today: Williston steam power and pumping plant

name: Buford-Trenton Project
note: A pump on a barge on the Missouri lifted river water about 30 feet into canals near Buford and Trenton, using power sent from Williston.
today: Buford-Trenton pumping plant (barge on the Missouri River)

name: Carlsbad Project
note: Reclamation bought a struggling private Pecos River canal system and rebuilt Avalon Dam by November 1907.

name: Sun River Project
note: The first unit was built on the former Fort Shaw military reservation west of Great Falls and first delivered water in 1909.

name: Orland Project
note: East Park Dam on Little Stony Creek stored water for the Sacramento Valley's first federal project, around the town of Orland.

name: Dakota National Forest
note: About 14,000 acres in today's Slope County, south of Medora, set aside around a rare stand of ponderosa pine and used as a tree nursery for prairie windbreaks. The only national forest ever established in North Dakota, it was abolished in 1917.

name: Garden City Forest Reserve
note: A tree-planting experiment on the high plains near Garden City, later renamed Kansas National Forest. Abolished in 1915.

name: Choctawhatchee National Forest
note: Longleaf pine forest on the Florida Panhandle. Transferred to the War Department in 1940; the land is now Eglin Air Force Base.
